author: kate-waddams
description: The planet grows more food than ever, and yet hunger is rising. The problem is not how much we produce, but how we grow, move and waste what we eat.

hero.hook: We grow enough to feed everyone. The problem is what we do with that food.

blocks.text: With hunger and [[malnutrition]] on the rise around the world, you could be forgiven for thinking the Earth no longer produces enough for a growing population. That is simply not true. Since the **1960s**, agricultural production has grown faster than the number of humans. What goes wrong is how that food is produced and distributed.

The figures clash. **7%** of children under five suffer from malnutrition, while **40%** of adults are overweight. And today, poor diet kills more adults than tobacco does. Feeding eight billion people is no easy task: the [[supply chain]] has gaps, we throw away staggering amounts of food, and many farming practices are no longer sustainable.

A farm captures sunlight and turns it into food. Plants do that work: once grown, they give us food we can eat. Livestock grazing on pasture, meanwhile, turn grass into meat and milk. Yet farms get a bad rap: degraded land, pollution, deforestation, animals competing with humans for food and space.

blocks.caption: Cows out at pasture: grass turned into milk and meat.

blocks.text: Those problems come partly from unsustainable farming practices. That is what needs to change. A common assumption says that growing ever more means pouring ever more into our production systems. It is false. Producing more does not necessarily require more pesticides, fertilizers, land or labor. It can even mean the opposite.

It all comes down to one word: efficiency. With more efficient farming methods, we can grow more food for billions of people while using fewer [[inputs]], meaning less fertilizer, fewer pesticides, less energy and less labor, and while taking up less land.

Growing enough is only half the battle. The food still has to reach consumers, a whole other challenge. The figure is dizzying: **one third** of the food produced worldwide is lost or wasted, some **1.3 billion tons** every year.

blocks.caption: Still-edible fruit and vegetables thrown out behind a supermarket.

blocks.text: The cost of [[food waste]] goes beyond the bin. Every apple thrown away also throws away the time, energy and money it took to grow it, harvest it and transport it.

With the [[globalization]] of agriculture, trade between continents and open markets, countries no longer rely on their own produce to feed their people. Some products are no longer seasonal: they are imported from all over the world. But that wider access lengthens supply chains, and the longer a chain, the more weak links it has.

sections.title: A third of all food never reaches the plate

blocks.text: Piling on more inputs to keep up with demand is neither sustainable nor practical. Farmers have to adopt better practices, and a growing population is not the only thing pushing them. They are already feeling climate change: erratic, unpredictable weather is forcing them to think outside the box.

Improving soil health, optimizing animal performance, planting climate-resistant crops, practicing [[precision agriculture]]: all are ways of making more from less. Rather than spreading fertilizer over a whole field, a robot analyzes the soil in real time and dispenses only the exact dose that patch needs. The result: lower costs, a smaller environmental footprint and better crop performance.

blocks.caption: A farm drone maps a field: precision agriculture measures out inputs meter by meter.

blocks.text: This kind of technology is part of the solution, and a growing area of agricultural research. To feed eight billion people, we do not necessarily need more land, more animals or more hectares of crops. We need to get more out of what we already use.

Farmers often get the blame. Yet they are the ones feeding our children, and they are also stewards of the countryside, responsible for the environment. But feeding the world is not their responsibility alone: it takes far more than growing food.

It asks us to make sustainable choices: to pick healthier, responsibly sourced produce, and to buy only what we will actually eat. The whole food industry, processors, packagers, transporters, marketers and we the consumers, can change its habits too. The future of food is a shared problem. The diets of eight billion people shape the entire planet, and you are part of that.
The Earth grows enough for everyone: feeding eight billion people means wasting less, producing more with fewer inputs and less land, and changing our choices, from the farm to the plate.

sections.title: A shared problem, from farm to consumer

sources.text: United Nations, Department of Economic and Social Affairs, « Can we feed the billions? ».
H. Ritchie, « No, growing more food does not mean we always need more and more inputs », Sustainability by Numbers.
